name: The Glasswater Hold

detectability.signature: perfectly flat chronometer baseline; the interior reads as one frozen instant held at constant phase

proximity: Time aboard visiting ships turns viscous; clocks lag and breaths feel long
Motion near the boundary smears, hands seeming to trail behind their gestures
contact: Objects entering cease motion entirely, preserved exactly as they crossed the line
Crew caught inside stand frozen mid-task, held in an interval too thin to measure
prolonged_exposure: Consciousness suspends between seconds, neither living nor dead until extraction
Nothing within ages, decays, or changes, however many centuries pass outside

phenomena: Interior contents existing in a single timeframe while the universe moves around them
Emerging ships appearing decades newer than their registry dates record
A glassy sheen over the whole sphere, like light trapped under ice
hazards: Desynchronization from normal spacetime upon exit
Equipment malfunction from timeline interference at the boundary layer
opportunities: Recovery of lost ships and crews in pristine condition
Unique research opportunity to study matter outside time's flow
Hidden base location, since the field conceals everything it holds
known_incidents: A rescue team boarded the clipper Salt Meridian and found her crew mid-meal, perfectly preserved two hundred years after her disappearance
description: The Glasswater Hold is a three-thousand-kilometer sphere of absolute stillness, its surface carrying a glassy luster like light caught beneath ice. Nothing inside it moves, glows, or decays; even tumbling wreckage hangs fixed at the instant of its crossing. Sensors return a chronometer baseline so flat that instrument techs initially suspected equipment failure.

The field neither pulses nor drifts, holding its contents at constant phase while stars wheel past. Vessels touching the boundary slow gradually, then stop altogether, their crews suspended mid-gesture rather than killed. Extraction teams working from outside can draw frozen objects back through the skin, where motion resumes without a heartbeat's interruption.

No civilization has claimed the Hold, though its geometry is too regular to be accidental and its age counts only four centuries. The recovery of the clipper Salt Meridian, her crew seated at a meal two centuries cold in every way but fact, made the field infamous among spacelaw judges. Inheritance disputes over the preserved are still working through the courts.

Salvage consortiums circle the Hold like gulls, arguing custody of everything its stillness keeps fresh, while ethicists fight over whether waking the preserved is rescue or something graver. Researchers beg for access to matter that has simply opted out of time. Whoever built it left no instructions, only a perfect pause.
